title: A quantum geometric mechanism for chiral domain wall metastability: Application to twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides
authors: Nisarg Chadha, Qiang Gao, Eslam Khalaf, Zhaoyu Han
abstract: Band topology can have an imprint on the excitations of a ferromagnet. A known example is quantum Hall ferromagnets and their lattice analogs; when both flavors have the same Chern number $C$, a smooth skyrmion texture binds charge $-eC$ per unit winding. Here, we consider instead the case of conjugate Chern bands related by time-reversal. We show that, despite the vanishing net charge response, a smooth texture can be associated with a dipole response---a domain wall (DW) with an in-plane winding along its length can bind a nonzero dipole density transverse to the wall. The strength of this dipole density is controlled by a dimensionless coefficient $c_G$. Although not quantized, the geometric dipole coefficient $c_G$ is a moment of the second Chern form of the occupied projector in mixed (momentum and order-parameter) space and is generally nonzero. The dipole-decorated DW can thus become metastable at a finite radius due to the competition between dipolar repulsion and the usual surface tension, even at a finite Zeeman field. In a realistic model of twisted MoTe$_2$, we find that $c_G$ drops sharply across a transition within the valley-polarized (VP) phase from a $C=1$ to a $C=0$ ferromagnet. This naturally explains recent pump-probe experiments~\cite{exp} at hole filling $ν=1$, in which a long-lived excitation survives reverse fields far exceeding the saturation field but disappears at an intermediate displacement field despite only weak changes in conventional magnetic diagnostics. Metastable spin textures thus serve as a sensitive probe of band quantum geometry, and as an intrinsic bottleneck for fast optical control of moiré ferromagnets in Chern-conjugate bands.
summary: The paper develops a theory showing that band topology dictates a dipole moment associated with chiral domain walls in ferromagnets. Applied to twisted TMDs, this geometric coefficient ($c_G$) predicts that the DW metastability is highly sensitive to topological phase transitions, offering a new diagnostic tool for probing quantum geometry in moiré materials.
main_problem: The study investigates how band topology, specifically through a geometric dipole moment, can stabilize chiral domain walls (DWs) in ferromagnets even when the net charge response vanishes.
main_result: A non-zero geometric dipole coefficient ($c_G$) leads to an energy cost that stabilizes DWs against collapse, and this coefficient is highly sensitive to topological phase transitions within twisted TMDs like tMoTe2.
method: The authors use symmetry-constrained Hartree-Fock methods on the occupied projector to calculate the mixed real-space–momentum-space second Chern form, which yields $c_G$.
model_or_system: The system is modeled using twisted transition-metal dichalcogenides (tTMDs) exhibiting conjugate Chern bands. The theory interpolates between Valence Polarized (VP) and Inter-Valley Coherent (IVC) states via a trial Hamiltonian $\hat{H}_{	ext{MF}}(\theta, \phi)$.
key_observables: Geometric dipole coefficient ($c_G$), transverse dipole density, domain wall energy $E(R)$, and the Chern number ($C$).
important_parameters: Twist angle ($\theta_M$), layer bias ($u_D$), Zeeman field strength, and the competition between dipolar repulsion and surface tension.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes an internal relative U(1) spin symmetry and time-reversal symmetry. Calculations are performed in the weak coupling regime for some analyses.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the dependence of $c_G$ on system parameters, showing sharp drops across topological transitions (e.g., $C=1$ to $C=0$) that correlate with changes in domain wall stability.
paper_structure: The paper establishes a theoretical framework linking band topology to dipole moments in DWs. It then applies this formalism to tTMDs, calculating $c_G$ using HF methods and demonstrating how its variation explains experimental observations of long-lived excitations near topological phase boundaries.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete example of how subtle quantum geometric invariants (like the second Chern form moment) can govern macroscopic stability properties (metastability) in condensed matter systems, linking topology directly to observable dynamics.
